nodes.title: Batching the queue at 15 minutes cuts human interruptions by 64% (25 gates to 9) and at one hour by 76% (to 6); the curve saturates at an hour, and 33% of gate arrivals already land within 60 seconds of the previous one
nodes.body:
w8-review-q-unmeasured lists four holes and says loom could close them with one schema change plus a planted-defect arm. Hole 3 is: 'no study reports total human minutes as a function of batching interval, so the 23-minute interruption cost has never been converted into a queue design.' e71 closes the half that is pure event arithmetic -- **how many times the loop demands attention**, as a function of how long it is allowed to accumulate.

The population: **60 attention asks** across 72 campaigns, by kind gate 25, anomaly 12, plateau 10, setup 8, holdout 3, stuck 1, infrastructure 1. All 60 were answered. Windows are aligned to the first arrival, which is the most favourable case for batching; a real scheduler would do worse, so every number below is a lower bound on interruptions.

Gate interruptions vs batching window: immediate **25**; 15 min **9** (-64%); 1 h **6** (-76%); 4 h **6** (-76%); 1 day **4** (-84%). For all asks together: 60 / 30 / 23 / 12 / 6. **The curve is essentially flat between 15 minutes and 4 hours** -- everything worth batching is already batched by an hour, and the remaining reduction to a day buys 2 more.

Why: arrivals are already clustered. Median gap between consecutive gate arrivals is **1,833 s**, but **33.3% of gaps are under 60 s** and **62.5% under 600 s**. The extreme case is `loom-graded2`, which raised 6 gates in about 4 minutes -- one campaign supplying 24% of all gate asks. So the loop is batching by accident: it raises a burst of alarms in one sitting, then goes quiet.

Dwell for the cost side: median **261 s**, 6 of 25 over an hour, 2 over 24 hours. Per-campaign gate asks: 11 campaigns ever asked, median 2, max 6.

What this does NOT establish: total human minutes. The ledger records when a checkpoint was raised and when it was answered, never how long anyone looked, and w8-review already found the 22.8-hour figure was a coincidence (6,684 changed lines divided by 300 lines/hour) rather than a measurement. So the queue design now has its x-axis (batching interval) and its y-axis (interruption count), and still no unit cost.
nodes.source: research/exp/e71.mjs over ~/.dsh/loom/campaigns/*/events.jsonl (60 checkpoint.raised, 25 gate, all answered)

nodes.title: The 23-minute interruption cost does not transfer to an idle supervisor: our dwell median is 4.3 minutes, which is shorter than the cost it would supposedly incur
nodes.body:
The literature constant everyone reaches for is 23 minutes to resume an interrupted task (Mark/Gudith/Klocke CHI 2008). The tempting calculation is 25 interruptions x 23 minutes = 9.6 hours of lost focus, cut to 2.3 hours by batching at an hour. e71 makes the interruption counts real, so that multiplication is now available -- and it should not be done, because its premise is absent.

That study interrupted people **who were already working on something else**. Our reviewer is not in flow: they are idle, the checkpoint arrives, they look at it, they decide. The evidence is the dwell distribution -- median **261 s**, i.e. **4.3 minutes**, and 40% under two minutes. A person who has just lost 23 minutes to a context switch does not come back in 4. The 23-minute number measures *recovery for someone who was doing something else*; our situation is asynchronous review, and the relevant cost is attention per decision, not recovery per interruption.

This matters because it changes the queue design's objective. If interruptions cost recovery time, batch aggressively and accept staleness. If interruptions cost a small fixed attention quantum each, then **the number that matters is decisions per unit of human time, and batching mostly helps by amortising the arrival**, not the recovery. Batching at an hour still wins -- 25 to 6 -- but for a different reason: it removes duplicate alarms about the same underlying state (six gates from one campaign), which is a redundancy argument, not a focus argument.

This is the fifth variant tonight of the same family: a published constant applied to a population it was not measured on. ana-027 (an agreement that was never at risk), exp-gap-011 (a tri-state read as boolean), exp-slo-002 (a cross product counted as events), ana-024 (absence in an append-only log is evidence about the writer), and now a recovery cost applied to someone who never recovered from anything. The mechanical check is the same one that would have caught all five: **name the population the constant was measured on, and assert our population is inside it** -- here, 'people mid-task' vs 'people idle', which one line of dwell data refutes.

Limits. The interruption counts are small (25 gates) and windows are aligned to first arrival, so the curve is descriptive, not a design rule. And nothing here says batching is free: six alarms answered as one batch may get one decision applied to six different situations, which is exactly the rubber-stamp risk w8-review measured (pass rate rising 30.1% to 36.8% under load).
nodes.source: research/exp/e71.mjs (dwell median 261 s); w8-review pass-rate drift; Mark/Gudith/Klocke CHI 2008 as cited in w2-human-interruption-cost

edges.note: hole 3 of the four: interruptions as a function of batching interval, which is the half that is event arithmetic rather than human minutes
quantifies the queue design the attention wave proposed: the curve saturates at an hour, so a 15-minute to 1-hour window is where all the value is
keeps the 23-minute figure as a fact about interrupted workers and shows our reviewers are not that population -- dwell median 4.3 minutes
that measured the review bill in changed lines (6,684 over 114 promotions); this measures the arrival rate of the same queue
dwell shorter than the cost it would incur is the falsifier for importing the interruption constant
same family: a published number applied to a population it was not measured on; here the population is 'idle supervisor' not 'interrupted worker'
that one argues interruption buys speed in agent supervision; the speed is real but the recovery-cost framing it inherits does not apply to an idle reviewer

gaps.title: What is the actual attention cost per gate decision, and can it be inferred from decision content rather than from clock time?
gaps.body: e71 gives interruptions; the missing unit is cost per interruption. Clock time cannot supply it (dwell is queue time, not reading time) and self-report is unreliable (w8-attention: 79% of missed silent defects were rated 4-5/5 confidence). The one channel that might work is the decision content itself: every answer carries a note, and a note that cites a specific artifact (a file, a test, a line, a verifier output) is evidence that the diff was read, while a note that only restates the card is evidence that it was not. Scoring notes by whether they mention something not present in the checkpoint payload is cheap and mechanical. What makes it non-trivial is that the notes are mine, so I would be scoring my own diligence -- but the asymmetry it would expose (do rejections cite artifacts more than approvals?) is exactly the rubber-stamp signal w8-review's pass-rate drift predicts, and it can be checked against an independent fact: whether the patch the approval landed ever had to be reverted.
